- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts are rising steadily, check for over-optimism — true outcomes often overshoot initial peaks then correct, especially after high-event days.
- If official event net supply is negative and sentiment is bearish, model forecasts tend to underestimate true price spikes — adjust upward by 2–5% for high-event periods.
- After a sharp spike in true outcome (e.g., >10% above prior 30d mean), model forecasts often lag or overshoot — apply a 1–3 day lag correction and reduce slope after peak.
- When sentiment is mixed or neutral (0.33–0.67), model forecasts often drift upward — apply downward bias correction of 1–3% to avoid overfitting to recent trends.
- In high-event periods (≥20 events/30d), true outcomes frequently deviate from linear trends — use exponential smoothing or moving average with 3–5 day window to capture volatility.
- If model forecasts are flat or rising slowly while sentiment is volatile, true outcomes often spike — adjust forecast to reflect sentiment volatility by adding 1–2% to forecast if sentiment >0.67.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, mean reversion is strong — if forecast is >10% above 30d mean, reduce by 1–3% unless event context strongly supports upside.
- When supply net is negative and bullish sentiment is high, model may overestimate price — reduce forecast by 1–3% to account for supply constraints.
- If sentiment is bearish and model forecasts are rising, apply downward bias — reduce forecast by 1–3% to avoid overconfidence in bullish signals.
- In high-event periods with low sentiment, true outcomes often spike — adjust forecast to reflect event-driven volatility, not trend.
